notes: Ruling slot 0 = KANU (MD has KANU in 13; ruling slot rule takes precedence, MD KANU sprite reused). Coalition slot 13 = Provincial Administration, Kenyatta's main instrument of rule. KPU (banned 30 Oct 1969, Odinga detained) placed in 18. KADU (merged into KANU 1964) kept as the pro-Western majimbo wing in slot 1. Mwambao United Front in 23 as the only monarchist current (Zanzibar Sultan's coastal strip).

0.name: Kenya African National Union
0.text:
The Kenya African National Union has led Kenya since independence in 1963 under President Jomo Kenyatta. Since the ban on the Kenya People's Union in October 1969 it is the only legal party, and in the December 1969 elections only KANU candidates stood, though many sitting members lost their seats in contested primaries.

KANU stands for African capitalism, the Africanization of land and trade, close ties with Britain and the United States and firm rejection of communism. Behind Kenyatta stand Vice-President Daniel arap Moi, the Kiambu inner circle and the provincial bosses. Its leverage lies in patronage, the state and Kenyatta's authority.

1.name: Kenya African Democratic Union
1.text:
The Kenya African Democratic Union was founded in 1960 by the smaller peoples of the Rift Valley, the Coast and Western Kenya, fearing Kikuyu and Luo dominance. It dissolved into KANU in 1964, but its leaders, above all Daniel arap Moi and Ronald Ngala, remain a recognizable bloc within the ruling party.

The former KADU men favour regional autonomy, protection of land rights of the Kalenjin, Maasai and coastal peoples, private enterprise and close ties with Britain. They are firmly anti-communist. Their leverage lies in Moi's vice-presidency, Rift Valley votes and their role as a counterweight to the Kikuyu establishment.

2.name: Law Society of Kenya
2.text:
The Law Society of Kenya is the statutory body of the country's advocates, still dominated by European and Asian lawyers but with a rising African membership. After the murder of Tom Mboya in July 1969, the ban on the KPU and the detention of its leaders, it is one of the few organized voices for the rule of law.

Its members defend detainees, call for an independent judiciary, open elections and restrictions on the Preservation of Public Security powers. They favour a market economy and Western ties. Their leverage lies in the courts, the press and the respect the profession still enjoys in Nairobi.

3.name: Central Organization of Trade Unions
3.text:
The Central Organization of Trade Unions was created by the government in 1965 to end the rivalry between the Western-backed Kenya Federation of Labour and its left-wing competitor. It is the only recognized labour centre and is closely watched by the Ministry of Labour.

COTU stands for collective bargaining, minimum wages, Africanization of skilled posts and workers' housing, within a framework of industrial peace set by the state. It shuns open politics but retains ties to the international free trade unions. Its leverage lies in the railways, the docks of Mombasa, plantations and the Nairobi industries.

4.name: Wajamaa wa Pinto
4.text:
Wajamaa wa Pinto are the hidden Marxist network that grew around Pio Gama Pinto, the socialist organizer murdered in 1965, and the short-lived Lumumba Institute, closed by the government the same year. Its members are trade unionists, journalists and graduates of Soviet and East European universities.

They want land nationalization, state ownership of banks and plantations, a vanguard party and alignment with the socialist camp. With the KPU banned and its leaders detained, they work underground through study circles and contacts with Eastern embassies. Their leverage lies in Soviet scholarships and the anger of the landless.

5.name: Bado Uhuru
5.text:
Bado Uhuru takes its name from Oginga Odinga's book Not Yet Uhuru and gathers radical students at University College, Nairobi, young teachers and unemployed school-leavers. Their anger has grown with Mboya's murder, the Kisumu shootings of October 1969 and the ban on the KPU.

They denounce the Kenyatta elite as a new class of landlords, demand free land for the poor, an end to foreign military ties and solidarity with liberation struggles in southern Africa. They organize demonstrations and leaflets rather than parties. Their leverage lies on campus and in the slums of Nairobi.

6.name: Itungati
6.text:
Itungati was the name of the rank-and-file Mau Mau fighters in the forests of Nyandarua and Mount Kenya. Today the surviving veterans, many still landless, feel betrayed: land has gone to former loyalists and the new elite, while they live as squatters on the edges of the settled farms.

They demand free land, recognition of the Land and Freedom Army and the expulsion of remaining European settlers, and distrust the Western capitalists courted by the government. They draw on oaths, clan ties and memories of the emergency. Their leverage lies in their moral authority in Central Province.

7.name: Special Branch
7.text:
The Special Branch of the Kenya Police, inherited from the colonial emergency apparatus, is the regime's political intelligence service. Under James Kanyotu it monitors the opposition, the trade unions, the universities and foreign embassies, and supervised the crackdown on the KPU in late 1969.

The Special Branch favours detention without trial, control of the press and a one-party state loyal to Kenyatta. It is wary of foreign influence of every kind. Its leverage lies in files, informers, the power to arrest and its direct line to State House.

8.name: Shia Imami Ismaili Community of Kenya
8.english: Shia Imami Ismaili Community of Kenya
8.text:
The Ismaili community of Kenya, followers of the Aga Khan, has jamatkhanas in Nairobi, Mombasa and Kisumu and runs schools, hospitals and the Nation newspaper group founded by Prince Karim Aga Khan in 1959.

The community stands for education, economic self-help, women's advancement and loyalty to the Kenyan state. It is worried by the Africanization of trade and the uncertain status of non-citizen Asians under the 1967 immigration law. Its leverage lies in capital, the press and a disciplined international network.

9.name: Africa Federation of Khoja Shia Ithna-Asheri Jamaats
9.english: Africa Federation of Khoja Shia Ithna-Asheri Jamaats
9.text:
The Africa Federation of Khoja Shia Ithna-Asheri Jamaats unites the Twelver Shia communities of East Africa, with strong jamaats in Mombasa, Nairobi and Lamu. Its members are Gujarati-speaking traders who follow the great clerical authorities of Najaf.

The federation insists on religious law, the authority of the marja and close communal discipline, sends students to Iraq and supports missionary work among Africans. It avoids politics but fears restrictions on non-citizen traders. Its leverage lies in coastal commerce, religious endowments and ties with Shia centres in Iraq and Iran.

10.name: Chief Kadhi of Kenya
10.text:
The office of the Chief Kadhi heads the Kadhi courts guaranteed to Kenya's Muslims by the 1963 independence settlement. Since 1968 it has been held by Sheikh Abdullah Saleh Farsy, a Zanzibari scholar and translator of the Koran into Swahili.

The Chief Kadhi stands for sharia in personal law, Muslim education and cooperation with the government in return for protection of Muslim rights. Farsy preaches a reformist Sunni Islam opposed to saint veneration. Its leverage lies in the courts, the mosques of the coast and the prestige of its holder.

11.name: Ummah ya Pwani
11.text:
Ummah ya Pwani is a small circle of young preachers and students in Mombasa and Lamu who returned from Medina and Cairo. They see the coast as a Muslim land absorbed against its will into a Christian-dominated state.

They call for a single Muslim community under sharia stretching across the Indian Ocean, reject secular law and the established sheikhs, and denounce the alcohol and tourism of the coast. They have no armed wing, but their sermons find ready listeners among unemployed youth. Their leverage lies in mosques of the old towns and contacts in the Arabian peninsula.

12.name: East African Muslim Welfare Society
12.text:
The East African Muslim Welfare Society was founded in Mombasa in 1945 with the support of the Aga Khan to build schools, mosques and clinics for African Muslims. In Kenya it remains the main Muslim development body, though its sister branches in Tanzania have been dissolved.

The society works for Muslim education, scholarships and social uplift, and lobbies for Muslim representation in government. It favours an Islam engaged with modern life and cooperation with Muslim states abroad. Its leverage lies in schools, welfare networks and funding from the Gulf and the Ismaili community.

13.name: Provincial Administration
13.text:
The Provincial Administration, the chain of provincial commissioners, district commissioners, chiefs and sub-chiefs inherited from colonial rule, is the backbone of Kenyatta's government. Answerable to the Office of the President, it largely bypasses KANU's own branches.

The administration keeps order, licenses meetings, settles land disputes and organizes self-help harambee projects. It favours strong central rule, development without politics and loyalty to the President rather than to the party. Its leverage lies in its presence in every location and its control over permits and land.

14.name: National Christian Council of Kenya
14.text:
The National Christian Council of Kenya, founded in 1943, unites the Protestant churches, from the Anglicans and Presbyterians to the Methodists and African-led churches. It runs schools, hospitals and development projects across the country.

The council stands for Christian morality, family life and national reconciliation, and has spoken against the oathing campaigns of 1969. It is cautious toward both the left and the government's excesses. Its leverage lies in congregations in every district and in the moral authority of its church leaders.

15.name: Kiambu Mafia
15.text:
The Kiambu Mafia is the circle of Kikuyu notables from Kenyatta's home district around Mbiyu Koinange, Minister of State in the Office of the President, and Njoroge Mungai, Minister of Defence. They control access to the President and to land, licences and loans.

They favour African capitalism, the purchase of settler estates by the well-connected, partnership with British and American companies and Kikuyu leadership of the succession. They oppose radicals and rival ethnic blocs. Their leverage lies in the President's ear, the land market and the state corporations.

16.name: Kenya National Chamber of Commerce
16.text:
The Kenya National Chamber of Commerce speaks for traders, importers and small businessmen, from Asian wholesalers in Nairobi to the growing African shopkeepers of the district towns.

It wants low taxes, free import licensing, credit for small traders and protection of private property. It opposes state trading monopolies, though its African members welcome the trade licensing laws that push Asian non-citizens out of rural markets. Its leverage lies in the retail trade and its contacts in the Ministry of Commerce.

17.name: East African Wild Life Society
17.text:
The East African Wild Life Society was founded in Nairobi in 1956 and is the leading conservation body in the region. Its members include wardens, zoologists, safari operators and wealthy patrons in Kenya and abroad.

The society campaigns against poaching and the ivory trade, pays for anti-poaching patrols and field studies, and backs national parks such as Tsavo and Nairobi. Its case is that wildlife tourism brings Kenya more foreign exchange than any crop. Its leverage lies in foreign donors, the safari trade and friends in the ministries.

18.name: Kenya People's Union
18.text:
The Kenya People's Union was founded in 1966 by Oginga Odinga after he resigned as Vice-President over KANU's turn to the right. After the riots during Kenyatta's visit to Kisumu in October 1969 it was banned, and Odinga and its other leaders are in detention.

The KPU demands free land for the landless, nationalization of key industries, an end to corruption and non-alignment with friendly ties to the socialist countries. Its base lies among the Luo of Nyanza, trade unionists and the urban poor. Its leverage lies in Odinga's popularity and widespread resentment of the regime.

19.name: Ardhi na Uhuru
19.text:
Ardhi na Uhuru, named after the slogan of the Mau Mau struggle, is the land-radical network of former freedom fighters, squatters and peasant activists who reject the market-based land transfer. Its best-known voice is Bildad Kaggia, one of the Kapenguru Six.

They demand the free redistribution of settler estates, cooperative farming on the Chinese and Tanzanian model and an end to the land-buying companies of the elite. They distrust both Moscow and Washington. Their leverage lies in Central Province, the Rift Valley squatter settlements and veterans' memories.

20.name: Muuma wa Gatundu
20.text:
Muuma wa Gatundu is the network behind the oathing campaign of mid-1969, when after Tom Mboya's murder thousands of Kikuyu were taken to Kenyatta's home at Gatundu to swear that the leadership would never leave the House of Mumbi.

The oath-takers stand for Kikuyu solidarity, the defence of land gained since independence and the exclusion of Luo politicians from power. Churches and opposition leaders condemn the campaign. Its leverage lies in local KANU branches, clan elders and fear of losing power after Kenyatta.

21.name: KANU Youth Wing
21.text:
The KANU Youth Wing grew out of the party's independence struggle and now serves as the ruling party's street force. Its members break up opposition meetings, enforce attendance at rallies and patrol markets, often in uniform.

The youth wingers preach loyalty to Kenyatta, hostility to the KPU, to Asians and to foreign critics, and demand jobs and land as reward. They are often used against students and trade unionists. Their leverage lies in numbers, intimidation and their protection by local politicians.

22.name: Kenya Armed Forces
22.text:
The Kenya Armed Forces, formed from the Kenya battalions of the King's African Rifles, include the Kenya Army, the Kenya Air Force and the Kenya Navy. After the mutiny of 1964 at Lanet, put down with British help, they have been carefully kept out of politics.

The officer corps is British-trained, with British advisers still present, and is engaged against Somali shifta in the North Eastern Province. It values professionalism, ethnic balance and loyalty to the President. Its leverage lies in being the ultimate guarantor of the regime.

23.name: Mwambao United Front
23.text:
The Mwambao United Front was formed around 1960 by Arab and Swahili notables of the ten-mile coastal strip, nominally under the sovereignty of the Sultan of Zanzibar until 1963. It campaigned for coastal autonomy or union with Zanzibar, but lost when the strip was joined to Kenya.

Since the 1964 revolution in Zanzibar and the exile of Sultan Jamshid bin Abdullah to Britain, its survivors keep a quiet loyalty to the dynasty and to coastal autonomy. They defend Arab and Swahili land titles and Muslim identity. Their leverage lies in old families of Mombasa, Malindi and Lamu.
